section_summary: The section opens with the conclusion, appendices, and bibliography of a Spanish-language study of Peru’s 1935 import-quota system, especially restrictions on foreign cotton textiles. It then presents newspaper clippings concerning Japanese landholdings, business organization, immigration, commercial competition, and both anti-Japanese and pro-Japanese arguments. The section closes with a confidential 1936 U.S. Embassy despatch analyzing Japanese propaganda in Peru, followed by the opening of an attached clipping on Japanese immigration.

subfiles.title: Conclusion, general assessment, appendices, and bibliography of a study on import contingents
subfiles.doc_type: Economic study with legal appendices and bibliography
subfiles.about: The closing portion of a study explains and documents Peru’s 1935 quota system for imported manufactured cotton goods.
subfiles.summary: The largely illegible opening pages contain the study’s conclusion and general assessment. Seven appendices reproduce the decree establishing national import quotas, supplementary quotas for Switzerland and Austria, a thirty-day extension, an exemption for Loreto, and administrative rules for operating the contingent system. A bibliography lists economic, legal, industrial, and international-labor sources used in the study.

subfiles.title: “Letter from Hajime Hoshi” and petition concerning the Tulumayo lands
subfiles.doc_type: Newspaper clipping containing a letter and legal petition
subfiles.to: Director of El Comercio; President of Peru
subfiles.about: Senshi Saito answers Pedro Figueroa San Miguel’s accusation that the Hajime Hoshi enterprise had usurped state lands in the Tulumayo region.
subfiles.summary: Saito asks El Comercio to publish his reply and December 9 petition on the Tulumayo lands' chain of title through the 1919 sale to Hajime Hoshi, attacking his accuser and asking costs and damages.

subfiles.title: “Se ha fundado una Asociación de Comerciantes Japoneses”
subfiles.from: Y. Watano, interviewed by an unnamed reporter
subfiles.about: Y. Watano explains the purposes of the newly organized Japanese Association of Commerce and Industries of Peru.
subfiles.summary: Interview: a new association of Japanese merchants in Peru will work on collective economic defense and trade promotion; Watano says trade volumes don't yet justify a Japanese bank.

subfiles.title: “Hagamos frente al peligro japonés”
subfiles.about: The editorial urges officials to block a Japanese-backed omnibus company from entering Lima’s transport business.
subfiles.summary: Editorial alleging a Japanese company, using a local front, seeks to run buses in Lima, another invasion of fields reserved for Peruvians; it demands official action.

subfiles.title: “La expansión asiática en el Perú”
subfiles.about: The article calls for legal restrictions on Asian immigration and Japanese acquisition or leasing of agricultural land.
subfiles.summary: Editorial citing an Arequipa association: Chinese and Japanese penetration is spreading to provinces, Japanese firms produce fifteen percent of cotton; it urges quotas and warns of a Japanese bank.

subfiles.title: “Atajemos la conquista amarilla”
subfiles.about: C. O. Martínez calls for nationalist legislation against Japanese economic and demographic expansion.
subfiles.summary: Martinez calls Japanese settlement a state within the state displacing Peruvian workers, urging a new immigration law and reciprocal treatment, in racially charged rhetoric.

subfiles.title: Notice refusing Japanese advertising
subfiles.about: La Ruta announces that it will accept no advertisements from Japanese-owned commercial, industrial, or agricultural firms.
subfiles.summary: Notice instructing advertising agents not to accept advertising from Japanese-owned concerns.

subfiles.title: “La Sociedad Nacional de Industrias apoya a la Cámara de Comercio del Cuzco contra la competencia textil japonesa”
subfiles.from: Augusto Maurer, Sociedad Nacional de Industrias
subfiles.about: The Sociedad Nacional de Industrias defends import quotas as protection against Japanese textile competition.
subfiles.summary: Maurer says the Cusco Chamber of Commerce supports the cotton textile quota system, whose limited results stem from late application, exemptions and Japan's large quota.

subfiles.title: “El Perú debiera organizar la inmigración japonesa”
subfiles.doc_type: Newspaper article reproducing a consular memoir
subfiles.about: Former consul Pedro E. Paulet argues that Peru should direct Japanese immigration toward colonization and vocational development in the Amazonian interior.
subfiles.summary: Paulet proposes organizing Japanese agricultural colonists for Peru's Amazonian interior, linked to anthracite exports and trade with Japan, and Japanese artisans to teach indigenous communities.

subfiles.title: “Los industriales japoneses nos conquistan”
subfiles.about: The editorial accuses Japanese artisans and small merchants of unfair competition, adulteration, and exploitation of working-class consumers.
subfiles.summary: The writer portrays Japanese traders and manufacturers as infiltrating Peruvian commerce with cheap, poor-quality goods and displacing national industry. Lima and Callao authorities are criticized for inadequate inspection of scales, prices, and merchandise. The article demands municipal regulation and stronger protection for Peruvian producers and consumers.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 4765: “Further report concerning Japanese Propaganda in Peru”
subfiles.from: Louis G. Dreyfus, Jr., U.S. Embassy, Lima
subfiles.to: U.S. Department of State, Washington, D.C.
subfiles.about: The U.S. Embassy reports on anti-Japanese journalism and Japanese efforts to cultivate goodwill and political influence in Peru.
subfiles.summary: Dreyfus reports that the press campaign focused on Japanese restaurants, clandestine immigration, plantation labor conditions, and violations of Peruvian employment laws, while suggesting that some papers used attacks or praise to solicit Japanese financial support. Japanese propaganda emphasized gifts and athletic events, including facilities for Lima and Callao and support for Peruvian Olympic teams. The despatch also recounts a former Peruvian consul general’s view that Japanese migrants retained strong national commitments and that Japan showed strategic interest in the Huallaga, the Amazon basin, and a hypothetical Pacific–Marañón canal.

subfiles.title: Clipping on “Japanese Immigration”
subfiles.about: The opening of an attached article warns that Japanese and Chinese immigrants are entering Peru and displacing national workers from small businesses.
subfiles.summary: Clipping fragment claiming Japanese ships bring penniless immigrants who monopolize retail trade and push Peruvian workers to Bolivia and Chile; continues beyond this section.
